Language Acquisition. The process by which children learn their native language or languages through exposure to speech in their social environment. Despite beginning with minimal vocabulary and simple structures, children rapidly master the grammar, pronunciation, and usage conventions of their native language within a few years. This achievement is remarkably consistent across cultures and conditions, suggesting both environmental input and innate biological predispositions shape the process.

Children follow a predictable developmental sequence. Cooing and babbling occur from zero to six months. First words appear at twelve to eighteen months. Two-word combinations emerge at eighteen to twenty-four months. Rapid vocabulary expansion happens around two to three years. And grammatical sophistication develops after three years. A vocabulary explosion occurs around age eighteen to twenty-four months when children suddenly accelerate from hundreds to thousands of words. The mechanism triggering this remains debated but suggests a qualitative shift in learning mechanisms. Children produce overgeneralizations, applying grammatical rules too broadly. They say "goed" instead of "went" and "two mouses" instead of "two mice." These mistakes reveal that children extract and apply rules rather than simply imitating speech.

Critical period evidence suggests exposure during early childhood is crucial. Children deprived of language input in early years face permanent difficulties acquiring full linguistic competence, even with later intensive instruction. Universal grammar, proposed by Noam Chomsky, posits that infants arrive with innate knowledge of grammatical principles, explaining how they acquire complex structures so rapidly from limited input. Steven Pinker and others argue children are innately prepared to learn language. The consistency of acquisition across cultures and the rapidity of learning suggest biological adaptation shaped by evolution. Bilingual children acquire multiple languages simultaneously during early childhood, demonstrating remarkable capacity. They keep languages partly separate, avoiding interference, while also showing cross-linguistic influence in specific features. Universal grammar represents the proposed innate linguistic knowledge driving acquisition. Steven Pinker is the cognitive scientist and author on language acquisition mechanisms. Cognitive development is the broader framework of mental development accompanying language learning. Developmental psychology is the discipline studying age-related changes including language acquisition. Generative grammar is the theoretical framework explaining how children master infinite sentence production. Innateness is the question of how much linguistic knowledge is inborn. Noam Chomsky is the linguist proposing universal grammar and innate linguistic capacity.
